claim: Biased integration remains a key challenge for gene therapy based on lentiviral vector technologies.
source: Biased integration remains a key challenge for gene therapy based on lentiviral vector technologies.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of gene therapy challenges, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In a previous paper (Cai et al., 2014a), the authors showed the use of integrase-defective lentiviral vectors (IDLVs) as carriers of complete gene repair kits consisting of zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN) proteins and repair sequences, allowing gene correction by homologous recombination (HR).
source: In a previous paper (Cai et al., 2014a), we showed the use of integrase-defective lentiviral vectors (IDLVs) as carriers of complete gene repair kits consisting of zinc-finger nuclease (ZFN) proteins and repair sequences, allowing gene correction by homologous recombination (HR).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: ZFN-loaded IDLVs insert transgenes by a homology-driven mechanism into safe loci.
source: Here, we follow this strategy to engineer ZFN-loaded IDLVs that insert transgenes by a homology-driven mechanism into safe loci.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The insertion mechanism is driven by time-restricted exposure of treated cells to ZFNs.
source: This insertion mechanism is driven by time-restricted exposure of treated cells to ZFNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ZFN degradation over time (Figure 1D).

claim: Targeted gene integration was shown in human stem cells, including CD34+ hematopoietic progenitors and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
source: We show targeted gene integration in human stem cells, including CD34+ hematopoietic progenitors and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Targeted insertions are identified in 89% of transduced iPSCs.
source: Notably, targeted insertions are identified in 89% of transduced iPSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing 34 out of 38 analyzed clones contained targeted insertions.

claim: Lentiviral vectors offer an effective gene delivery route, but also suffer from prevalent gene insertion into transcriptionally active regions.
source: Lentiviral vectors offer an effective gene delivery route, but also suffer from prevalent gene insertion into transcriptionally active regions (Schröder et al., 2002; Modlich et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TGI using lentiviral vectors can be achieved by delivering donor sequences for insertion by homologous recombination (HR) into double-strand breaks (DSBs) generated by tailored endonucleases.
source: TGI using lentiviral vectors can be achieved by delivering donor sequences for insertion by homologous recombination (HR) into double-strand breaks (DSBs) generated by tailored endonucleases (Lombardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Genetic operations involving TGI in stem cells are challenged by low membrane permeability, low HR efficiency, and high sensitivity to external manipulation.
source: Development of programmable nucleases, ZFNs, TALENs, and now CRISPR/Cas9, has made effective gene disruption feasible, even in stem cells, but genetic operations involving TGI in stem cells are still challenged by low membrane permeability, low HR efficiency, and high sensitivity to external manipulation (Genovese et al., 2014; Hockemeyer et al., 2011; Hendel et al., 2015; Tay et al., 2013; Tiyaboonchai et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Approximately 5000 copies of Gag and GagPol polypeptides form the capsid of lentiviral vectors.
source: Together with a dimer of lentiviral vector RNAs, approximately 5000 copies of Gag and GagPol polypeptides (of which about half carry a ZFN fused to the matrix protein) form the capsid, which is wrapped in a segment of the membrane during budding from the producer cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the composition of lentiviral particles, based on established knowledge.

claim: About half of the Gag and GagPol polypeptides carry a ZFN fused to the matrix protein.
source: Together with a dimer of lentiviral vector RNAs, approximately 5000 copies of Gag and GagPol polypeptides (of which about half carry a ZFN fused to the matrix protein) form the capsid, which is wrapped in a segment of the membrane during budding from the producer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design where equal amounts of ZFN-fused and non-fused constructs were used.

claim: ZFNs are released from Gag and GagPol upon cleavage by the viral protease during maturation of the virus particle.
source: ZFNs are released from Gag and GagPol upon cleavage by the viral protease during maturation of the virus particle.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of lentiviral particle maturation.

claim: The mature virus particles contain two types of ZFNs, left and right, which upon DNA binding in the target cell form a catalytically active dimer.
source: The mature virus particles contain two types of ZFNs, left and right, which upon DNA binding in the target cell form a catalytically active dimer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ZFN function and the experimental design.

claim: After viral entry in the target cells and endosomal escape, vector RNA is reverse transcribed to DNA, which can serve as donor for homology-directed insertion at targeted breakage sites generated by the co-delivered ZFNs.
source: After viral entry in the target cells and endosomal escape, vector RNA is reverse transcribed to DNA, which can serve as donor for homology-directed insertion at targeted breakage sites generated by the co-delivered ZFNs (Figure 1A, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ZFNs were highly enriched at the cell membrane of producer cells.
source: By staining with an antibody specific for the tag, we found that the ZFNs were highly enriched at the cell membrane (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For both LP-HA-ZFN(gfp) and LP-eGFP, co-localization of the fusion protein with viral p24 protein was observed.
source: We then visualized the lentiviral particles (designated LPs since the vector was not included) and found for both LP-HA-ZFN(gfp) and LP-eGFP co-localization of the fusion protein with viral p24 protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that ZFN (or eGFP) proteins were indeed packaged into the LPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: ZFN proteins were packaged into the lentiviral particles.
source: We then visualized the lentiviral particles (designated LPs since the vector was not included) and found for both LP-HA-ZFN(gfp) and LP-eGFP co-localization of the fusion protein with viral p24 protein (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that ZFN (or eGFP) proteins were indeed packaged into the LPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data.

claim: Within the first hour after exposure to LP-HA-ZFN(gfp), the ZFNs were easily detectable inside the cells.
source: Already within the first hour after exposure to LP-HA-ZFN(gfp), the ZFNs were easily detectable inside the cells, whereas after 24 hr essentially all ZFNs had been degraded or diluted (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After 24 hr, essentially all ZFNs had been degraded or diluted.
source: Already within the first hour after exposure to LP-HA-ZFN(gfp), the ZFNs were easily detectable inside the cells, whereas after 24 hr essentially all ZFNs had been degraded or diluted (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nucleases delivered by LPs were immediately available after transduction.
source: These findings showed that nucleases delivered by LPs were immediately available after transduction and that the time of action was restricted due to decay of the proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course data showing ZFN presence within 1 hour.

claim: The time of action of nucleases was restricted due to decay of the proteins.
source: These findings showed that nucleases delivered by LPs were immediately available after transduction and that the time of action was restricted due to decay of the proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course data showing ZFN degradation by 24 hours.

claim: Three days post-transduction, a higher frequency of eGFP+ cells was observed among cells transduced with IDLV/egfp than for cells transduced with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp (59.1% versus 44.7%).
source: Initially, three days post-transduction, a higher frequency of eGFP+ cells was observed among cells transduced with IDLV/egfp than for cells transduced with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp (59.1% versus 44.7%), indicating that the overall transduction potential was higher for IDLVs that did not carry ZFNs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The overall transduction potential was higher for IDLVs that did not carry ZFNs.
source: Initially, three days post-transduction, a higher frequency of eGFP+ cells was observed among cells transduced with IDLV/egfp than for cells transduced with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp (59.1% versus 44.7%), indicating that the overall transduction potential was higher for IDLVs that did not carry ZFNs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher percentage of eGFP+ cells at early time points.

claim: At later time points, 2.5% of the cells were eGFP+ after treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, whereas the percentage dropped to below 1% in IDLV/egfp-treated cells.
source: Nevertheless, at later time points 2.5% of the cells were eGFP+ after treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, whereas the percentage dropped to below 1% in IDLV/egfp-treated cells (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Events of correct integration into AAVS1 locus were evident after treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp.
source: PCR amplification and sequencing of the 5' and 3' junction sites including part of the donor sequence and the regions flanking the inserted transgene cassette showed that events of correct integration into AAVS1 locus were evident after treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, whereas PCR products indicative of site-directed insertion did not appear for IDLV/egfp (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PCR products indicative of site-directed insertion did not appear for IDLV/egfp.
source: PCR amplification and sequencing of the 5' and 3' junction sites including part of the donor sequence and the regions flanking the inserted transgene cassette showed that events of correct integration into AAVS1 locus were evident after treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, whereas PCR products indicative of site-directed insertion did not appear for IDLV/egfp (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mismatches introduced by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) were detected in 5% of the AAVS1 alleles.
source: However, DSBs were not repaired by HR only, and mismatches introduced by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) were detected in 5% of the AAVS1 alleles, as measured by Surveyor nuclease assay (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Fluc gene expression was maintained for up to 18 days after transduction with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/fluc.
source: Indeed, fluc gene expression was maintained for up to 18 days after transduction with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/fluc (Figure 1H), although the levels dropped from the initial 3-day time point, where episomal forms were still likely to support expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: For IDLV/fluc, luminescence dropped to almost undetectable levels.
source: For IDLV/fluc, in contrast, luminescence dropped to almost undetectable levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: TGI of the fluc gene into the AAVS1 locus was verified by PCR.
source: TGI of the fluc gene into the AAVS1 locus was verified by PCR (Figure 1I), and the rate of NHEJ estimated to be 8% (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The rate of NHEJ for IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/fluc was estimated to be 8%.
source: TGI of the fluc gene into the AAVS1 locus was verified by PCR (Figure 1I), and the rate of NHEJ estimated to be 8% (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Among 16 clones generated with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/puro, a 2.2-kb fragment, indicative of precise TGI by HR, was detected in 11 clones.
source: Among 16 clones generated with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/puro, a 2.2-kb fragment, indicative of precise TGI by HR, was detected in 11 clones (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Two clones (clone 5 and clone 13) showed a 3.7-kb band, suggesting that the full-length lentiviral DNA in these two cases was captured and inserted by chance into the ZFN-induced DSB at the AAVS1 locus.
source: Notably, two clones (clone 5 and clone 13) showed a 3.7-kb band, and these clones therefore were among clones that were analyzed by Southern blotting using another restriction enzyme and an AAVS1-specific probe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and 1G). A common 6.4-kb band was observed for clones 5 and 13 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that the full-length lentiviral DNA in these two cases was captured and inserted by chance into the ZFN-induced DSB at the AAVS1 locus.
evidence: This is inferred from Southern blot data showing specific band patterns.

claim: Site-directed gene insertion into ZFN-generated DSBs also occurred, although less frequently, in an HR-independent fashion.
source: These findings demonstrated that site-directed gene insertion into ZFN-generated DSBs also occurred, although less frequently, in an HR-independent fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the Southern blot data showing non-HR integration events.

claim: 84% (26/31) of the analyzed clones contained a targeted insertion of the puro gene in the AAVS1 locus.
source: We analyzed 15 additional puromycin-resistant clones by PCR and found that 13 out of these clones yielded PCR products indicative of TGI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H). In total, 84% (26/31) of the analyzed clones contained a targeted insertion of the puro gene in the AAVS1 locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data from multiple clones.

claim: The fragments detected by Southern blot analysis of IDLV/puro-treated clones had variable sizes, indicating that the integrations were random events that occurred at different genomic locations.
source: In contrast, the fragments detected by Southern blot analysis of IDLV/puro-treated clones had variable sizes (Figure 1M), indicating that the integrations were random events that occurred at different genomic locations.
evidence: This is inferred from Southern blot data showing variable band sizes.

claim: ZFN-loaded VSV-G-pseudotyped LPs loaded with AAVS1-directed ZFNs resulted in targeted cleavage upon transduction of CD34+ cells.
source: We first verified that ZFN-loaded VSV-G-pseudotyped LPs loaded with AAVS1-directed ZFNs resulted in targeted cleavage upon transduction of CD34+ cells. Hence, indels introduced through repair by NHEJ were found in 5% of the alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data.

claim: Indels introduced through repair by NHEJ were found in 5% of the alleles in CD34+ cells transduced with LP-ZFN(AAVS1).
source: We first verified that ZFN-loaded VSV-G-pseudotyped LPs loaded with AAVS1-directed ZFNs resulted in targeted cleavage upon transduction of CD34+ cells. Hence, indels introduced through repair by NHEJ were found in 5% of the alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The presence of EF-C allowed transduction of 85.1% of CD34+ cells with a standard eGFP-encoding lentiviral vector.
source: In our setting, the presence of EF-C allowed transduction of 85.1% of the cells with a standard eGFP-encoding lentiviral vector, whereas between 27.5 and 30.8% of the cells were transduced in the presence of RetroNectin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Between 27.5 and 30.8% of CD34+ cells were transduced in the presence of RetroNectin.
source: In our setting, the presence of EF-C allowed transduction of 85.1% of the cells with a standard eGFP-encoding lentiviral vector, whereas between 27.5 and 30.8% of the cells were transduced in the presence of RetroNectin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp resulted in (0.49 ± 0.14)% eGFP+ cells on average.
source: On average, treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp resulted in (0.49 ± 0.14)% eGFP+ cells, which was significantly higher than the percentage of eGFP+ cells (0.07 ± 0.03)% measured after transduction with the IDLV/egfp control without ZFNs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentage of eGFP+ cells after IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp treatment was significantly higher than after IDLV/egfp treatment in CD34+ cells.
source: On average, treatment with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp resulted in (0.49 ± 0.14)% eGFP+ cells, which was significantly higher than the percentage of eGFP+ cells (0.07 ± 0.03)% measured after transduction with the IDLV/egfp control without ZFNs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PCR analyses confirmed events of TGI by IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, but not by IDLV/egfp in CD34+ cells.
source: PCR analyses confirmed events of TGI by IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp, but not by IDLV/egfp (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp transduction only slightly affected the cell viability of CD34+ cells.
source: Notably, IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp transduction only slightly affected the cell viability (Figure 2D), and cell proliferation was not disturbed by the virus treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cell proliferation was not disturbed by IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp treatment in CD34+ cells.
source: Notably, IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp transduction only slightly affected the cell viability (Figure 2D), and cell proliferation was not disturbed by the virus treatment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Using protocol 2, the percentage of eGFP+ cells was increased to (0.98 ± 0.13)% after transduction with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp.
source: Indeed, using this improved protocol 2 (Figure 2A, green labeling), we were able to increase the percentage of eGFP+ cells to (0.98 ± 0.13)% after transduction with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TGI in the bulk of CD34+ cells was confirmed by PCR analysis using protocol 2.
source: Also based on this protocol, TGI in the bulk was confirmed by PCR analysis (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp treatment did not compromise the colony-forming capacity of CD34+ cells.
source: Notably, IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/egfp treatment did not compromise the colony-forming capacity of CD34+ cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony-forming assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Three eGFP+ colonies were identified out of a total of 302 analyzed colonies from CD34+ cells.
source: In accordance with the flow cytometry data, three eGFP+ colonies (example shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) were identified out of a total of 302 analyzed colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by colony analysis data.

claim: LP-ZFN(AAVS1) disrupted 4% of the targeted alleles in iPSCs.
source: LP-ZFN(AAVS1) and LP-ZFN(CCR5) disrupted 4% and 8%, respectively, of the targeted alleles in iPSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LP-ZFN(CCR5) disrupted 8% of the targeted alleles in iPSCs.
source: LP-ZFN(AAVS1) and LP-ZFN(CCR5) disrupted 4% and 8%, respectively, of the targeted alleles in iPSCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Surveyor nuclease assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Approximately 500 puromycin-resistant clones formed from 50,000 transduced iPSCs with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/puro.
source: Of the approximately 500 puromycin-resistant clones formed from 50,000 transduced iPSCs (Figure 3B), we initially randomly picked, isolated and expanded eight clones (clones 1–8) for further analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by colony counting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TGI had occurred in 19 out of 23 iPSC clones analyzed by PCR.
source: PCR amplification of the 5' and 3' junction sites showed that TGI had occurred in 19 out of the 23 clones (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Southern blot analysis confirmed that 11 of 15 clones (clones 9-23) contained an AAVS1-directed insertion.
source: Findings based on Southern blot analysis of clones 9–23 were consistent with the PCR analysis and confirmed that 11 of these 15 clones contained an AAVS1-directed insertion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Eight out of the 11 clones harbored a precise, homology-directed transgene insertion.
source: Eight out of the 11 clones harbored a precise, homology-directed transgene insertion, whereas only one of the two junction sites in the remaining 3 clones (clones 9, 17, and 18) was intact.
evidence: This is inferred from Southern blot and PCR data.

claim: Site-directed insertion in clones 9, 17, and 18 involved both HR and NHEJ.
source: Hence, the 5' junction site was intact in clone 17, whereas clones 9 and 18 contained an intact 3' junction site, indicating that site-directed insertion in these cases involved both HR and NHEJ.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of only one intact junction site.

claim: Sequence analysis of clones 1–8 showed junction sequences indicative of precise, homology-driven insertion.
source: Sequence analysis of the 5' and 3' junction sites amplified from clones 1–8 showed junctions sequences indicative of precise, homology-driven insertion (Figure 3E and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Clone 7 contained TGI in both alleles.
source: For one particular clone, clone 7, we were not able to amplify the 469-bp AAVS1 fragment, suggesting that both alleles in this clone contained a TGI (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to amplify the wild-type AAVS1 fragment.

claim: Sequencing of the AAVS1 locus provided evidence of biallelic cleavage in at least one of the clones (clone 5), resulting in a 1-bp insertion in the allele that did not contain the transgene.
source: Interestingly, sequencing of the AAVS1 locus provided evidence of biallelic cleavage in at least one of the clones (clone 5), resulting in a 1-bp insertion in the allele that did not contain the transgene (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data in Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Stemness of TGI-modified iPSCs was verified by characterization using alkaline phosphatase (AP) and the TRA-1-60 pluripotency marker.
source: Stemness of TGI-modified iPSCs was verified by characterization of a single representative clone using alkaline phosphatase (AP) and the TRA-1-60 pluripotency marker (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by staining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Genomic integrity was confirmed by karyotyping.
source: Also, genomic integrity was confirmed by karyotyping (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by karyotyping data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Indels were not identified in any of the three top-ranked off-target sites in clones 1–8.
source: To detect potential off-target cleavage by the virus-delivered ZFNs, we first sequenced the three top-ranked off-target sites in clones 1–8, but did not identify indels in any of these loci (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: 3% of the AAVS1 alleles that were not already targeted by transgene insertion contained indels in a pool of iPSC clones.
source: Among this pool of clones, most of which carry an AAVS1-directed gene insertion, we were not able to detect indels at off-target positions, whereas 3% of the AAVS1 alleles that were not already targeted by transgene insertion contained indels (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Indels were not detected at off-target positions in a pool of iPSC clones carrying AAVS1-directed gene insertions.
source: Among this pool of clones, most of which carry an AAVS1-directed gene insertion, we were not able to detect indels at off-target positions, whereas 3% of the AAVS1 alleles that were not already targeted by transgene insertion contained indels (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: At least one TGI event occurred in 19 of 23 analyzed iPSC clones treated with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/puro.
source: Altogether, our findings demonstrated high levels of ZFN specificity and precise TGI in the AAVS1 locus in iPSCs treated with IDLV-ZFN(AAVS1)/puro vectors, resulting in at least one TGI event in 19 of 23 analyzed iPSC clones.
evidence: This is a summary of the PCR and Southern blot data.

claim: The transgene cassette in all 15 clones (100%) treated with IDLV-ZFN(CCR5)/puro had been inserted site-specifically into the CCR5 locus.
source: Among the puromycin-resistant clones, we randomly picked, isolated and expanded 15 clones (clones 1–15) and showed by PCR analysis of each of these colonies that the transgene cassette in all 15 clones (100%) had been inserted site-specifically into the CCR5 locus (Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Approximately 19% of the CCR5 alleles that did not already carry a TGI contained an indel.
source: Notably, we identified an indel in approximately 19% of the CCR5 alleles that did not already carry a TGI, demonstrating that the second CCR5 allele was cleaved by ZFNs in approximately one of every five clones harboring a CCR5-directed insertion.
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Off-target cleavage and indel formation by NHEJ was not evident in any of the nine analyzed off-target candidate loci for CCR5-targeted ZFNs.
source: Importantly, off-target cleavage and indel formation by NHEJ was not evident in any of the nine analyzed off-target candidate loci.
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The CCR2 locus, which is highly homologous to the CCR5 site and a known off-target cleavage site for CCR5-targeted ZFNs, did not harbor detectable levels of indels.
source: Hence, not even the CCR2 locus (off-target 3), which is highly homologous to the CCR5 site and a known off-target cleavage site for CCR5-targeted ZFNs, harbored detectable levels of indels.
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Lentivirus-based co-delivery of nuclease proteins and a HR donor represents a powerful and safe approach for inserting transgenes into predetermined 'safe harbors' in the human genome.
source: In conclusion, lentivirus-based co-delivery of nuclease proteins and a HR donor represents a powerful and safe approach for inserting transgenes into predetermined 'safe harbors' in the human genome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: On average, four out of five lentiviral integrations land in genes.
source: On average, four out of five lentiviral integrations land in genes (Mitchell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including addition of a DNA-binding zinc-finger protein to the integrase.
source: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including (i) addition of a DNA-binding zinc-finger protein to the integrase (Bushman and Miller, 1997), (ii) fusion of a chromosomal binding domain to LEDGF, a cellular co-factor of the integrase (Gijsbers et al., 2010), and (iii) insertion of lentiviral DNA intermediates by transposases and recombinases (Vink et al., 2009; Staunstrup et al., 2009; Moldt et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including fusion of a chromosomal binding domain to LEDGF, a cellular co-factor of the integrase.
source: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including (i) addition of a DNA-binding zinc-finger protein to the integrase (Bushman and Miller, 1997), (ii) fusion of a chromosomal binding domain to LEDGF, a cellular co-factor of the integrase (Gijsbers et al., 2010), and (iii) insertion of lentiviral DNA intermediates by transposases and recombinases (Vink et al., 2009; Staunstrup et al., 2009; Moldt et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including insertion of lentiviral DNA intermediates by transposases and recombinases.
source: Different strategies have been employed to reprogram the integration machinery of lentiviral vectors including (i) addition of a DNA-binding zinc-finger protein to the integrase (Bushman and Miller, 1997), (ii) fusion of a chromosomal binding domain to LEDGF, a cellular co-factor of the integrase (Gijsbers et al., 2010), and (iii) insertion of lentiviral DNA intermediates by transposases and recombinases (Vink et al., 2009; Staunstrup et al., 2009; Moldt et al., 2011; Cai et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous strategies successfully alter the integration preference, but do not allow site-specific insertion into a preferred locus.
source: These approaches successfully alter the integration preference, but do not allow site-specific insertion into a preferred locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of previous approaches cited.

claim: The 'all-in-one' vector system can guide lentiviral cargo toward a safe harbor in up to 84% of HEK293T cells that were transduced.
source: By co-packaging designer nucleases and donor sequences into lentiviral vectors and utilizing cellular HR repair pathways to integrate the transgene, we can guide lentiviral cargo toward a safe harbor in up to 84% of HEK293T cells and 89% of iPSCs that were transduced with the 'all-in-one' vector system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing 26/31 clones with targeted insertion.

claim: The 'all-in-one' vector system can guide lentiviral cargo toward a safe harbor in up to 89% of iPSCs that were transduced.
source: By co-packaging designer nucleases and donor sequences into lentiviral vectors and utilizing cellular HR repair pathways to integrate the transgene, we can guide lentiviral cargo toward a safe harbor in up to 84% of HEK293T cells and 89% of iPSCs that were transduced with the 'all-in-one' vector system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data showing 34/38 clones with targeted insertion.

claim: The efficiency may likely be further improved by exploiting heterodimer-forming rather than homodimer-forming FokI domains.
source: The efficiency may likely be further improved by exploiting heterodimer-forming rather than homodimer-forming FokI domains (Doyon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, supported by a citation.

claim: TGI into the AAVS1 and CCR5 loci of stem cells has previously been achieved using HR-based strategies exploiting two- or three-component systems.
source: TGI into the AAVS1 and CCR5 loci of stem cells has previously been achieved using HR-based strategies exploiting two- or three-component systems based on delivery of plasmids, IDLVs, and baculovirus vectors as well as combinations of mRNA encoding ZFNs and IDLVs serving as the HR donor (Lombardo et al., 2011; Genovese et al., 2014; Tay et al., 2013; Tiyaboonchai et al., 2014; Hockemeyer et al., 2009; Lei et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Existing technologies for TGI in stem cells remain insufficient and highly toxic.
source: Despite the potential of genetic therapies based on TGI in stem cells, like CD34+ cells and iPSCs, existing technologies remain insufficient and highly toxic (Genovese et al., 2014; Hoban et al., 2015; Merling et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TGI in CD34+ cells transduced with ZFN-loaded IDLVs did not affect the viability, proliferation, or colony-forming capacity of the cells.
source: Exploiting the capacity of lentiviruses to co-deliver nucleases and a transgene cassette, we showed TGI in CD34+ cells transduced with ZFN-loaded IDLVs without affecting the viability, proliferation, or colony-forming capacity of the cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D, 2E, and 2H.

claim: A selective growth advantage of the TGI-engineered cells would be required for successful engraftment in CD34+ cells.
source: However, the efficiency was only modest, suggesting that a selective growth advantage of the TGI-engineered cells, as in SCID-X1, would be required for successful engraftment.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the modest efficiency observed.

claim: Efficacy could be boosted by combining virus treatment with exposure to chemicals enhancing stem cell self-renewal, by supplying NHEJ inhibitors, or by manipulating cell cycle conditions in favor of HR.
source: Possibly, efficacy could be boosted by combining virus treatment with exposure to chemicals enhancing stem cell self-renewal, by supplying NHEJ inhibitors (Chu et al., 2015), or by manipulating cell cycle conditions in favor of HR (Marniemi et al., 1975).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential improvements, with some support from citations.

claim: Stable transduction rates with ZFN-loaded IDLVs leading to TGI are reduced relative to conventional lentiviral gene delivery strategies.
source: Stable transduction rates with ZFN-loaded IDLVs leading to TGI are undoubtedly reduced relative to conventional lentiviral gene delivery strategies.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lower initial transduction rates for ZFN-loaded vectors.

claim: A few clones contained an additional, randomly inserted transgene cassette.
source: Also, as typically observed in relation to the standard use of IDLVs, we found that a few clones contained an additional, randomly inserted transgene cassette, which could be of relevance for potential future therapeutic use.
evidence: This is inferred from the Southern blot data showing additional bands in some clones.

claim: Lentiviral ZFN protein delivery did not lead to detectable off-target cleavage.
source: Importantly, however, we found that lentiviral ZFN protein delivery did not lead to detectable off-target cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by next-generation sequencing data shown in Figures 3H and 3L.

claim: Lentiviral delivery of site-targeted endonucleases supports safer engineering of the genome compared to other delivery strategies.
source: This is in contrast to higher levels of CCR2 targeting reported in previous studies using other delivery strategies based on adenoviral vectors, plasmid transfection, or administration of recombinant proteins (Perez et al., 2008; Gaj et al., 2012), suggesting that lentiviral delivery of site-targeted endonucleases supports safer engineering of the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with previous studies showing higher off-target effects.

claim: Lentivirus particles can ferry programmable nucleases, facilitating homology-driven, site-directed genomic insertion of a co-delivered transgene.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that lentivirus particles can ferry programmable nucleases, facilitating homology-driven, site-directed genomic insertion of a co-delivered transgene.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Co-delivery of nucleases and donor sequences ensures time-limited exposure of the treated cell to nucleases.
source: Such co-delivery ensures time-limited exposure of the treated cell to nucleases and, yet, results in frequent TGI with particular applicability in iPSCs.
evidence: This is supported by the ZFN lifespan data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Co-delivery of nucleases and donor sequences results in frequent TGI with particular applicability in iPSCs.
source: Such co-delivery ensures time-limited exposure of the treated cell to nucleases and, yet, results in frequent TGI with particular applicability in iPSCs.
evidence: This is supported by the high efficiency data in iPSCs shown in Figure 3.
